current_authoritative_paper.authors: Fabrizio Guillaro; Vincenzo De Rosa; Davide Cozzolino; Luisa Verdoliva

current_authoritative_paper.abstract: Significant progress has been made in detecting synthetic images, however most existing approaches operate on a single image instance and overlook a key characteristic of real-world dissemination: as viral images circulate on the web, multiple near-duplicate versions appear and lose quality due to repeated operations like recompression, resizing and cropping. As a consequence, the same image may yield inconsistent forensic predictions based on which version has been analyzed. In this work, to address this issue we propose QuAD (Quality-Aware calibration with near-Duplicates) a novel framework that makes decisions based on all available near-duplicates of the same image. Given a query, we retrieve its online near-duplicates and feed them to a detector: the resulting scores are then aggregated based on the estimated quality of the corresponding instance. By doing so, we take advantage of all pieces of information while accounting for the reduced reliability of images impaired by multiple processing steps. To support large-scale evaluation, we introduce two datasets: AncesTree, an in-lab dataset of 136k images organized in stochastic degradation trees that simulate online reposting dynamics, and ReWIND, a real-world dataset of nearly 10k near-duplicate images collected from viral web content. Experiments on several state-of-the-art detectors show that our quality-aware fusion improves their performance consistently, with an average gain of around 8% in terms of balanced accuracy compared to plain average. Our results highlight the importance of jointly processing all the images available online to achieve reliable detection of AI-generated content in real-world applications. Code and data are publicly available at https://grip-unina.github.io/QuAD/

contributions.method: QuAD calibrates detector logits conditioned on no-reference image quality and aggregates evidence over related near-duplicates. It fits class-specific linear means and log variances with eight coefficients using maximum likelihood. It does not introduce a newly trained base image detector.
contributions.resource: Two separately named grouped-image resources with explicit construction and retrieval rules are declared contributions. ReWIND supplies genuine web repostings and AncesTree supplies controlled known degradation trees; both support analyses beyond the proposed calibration rule.
contributions.locator: Contribution list p.2; Section3 pp.3–4; Sections4–5 pp.4–8.

question_matrix.question: What do AncesTree and ReWIND represent?
question_matrix.finding: AncesTree is a controlled collection of related degraded versions organized as stochastic trees. ReWIND is a curated real-web collection of near-duplicates of viral real and AI-generated images. They address version-dependent authenticity decisions; neither is merely a list of the QuAD detector outputs.

question_matrix.question: Are the two resources new rather than renamed existing datasets or ordinary perturbation variants?
question_matrix.finding: ReWIND reuses known source images but expands their online near-duplicate retrieval and adds fact-checked sources; it is a new assembled collection, not wholly new source content. AncesTree deliberately uses simulated perturbations, but contributes a systematic multilevel branching degradation structure whose distributions are motivated by ReWIND. Originality is in curation, grouping and controlled histories, not an unsupported assertion that every root image or generator output was newly created.
question_matrix.locator: Contribution list p.2; Section 3 pp.3–4; Table 1; Figure 5.

question_matrix.question: How many source images exist and what is their provenance?
question_matrix.finding: AncesTree starts from 100 real RAISE images and 1,000 semantically aligned synthetic counterparts across ten named generator families, then generates 124 non-root variants per source: 1,100×124=136,400. The source paragraph explicitly credits previously provided synthetic material to Synthbuster [1] and B-Free [12]. ReWIND contains 162 source groups, 87 real and 75 fake, comprising 9,646 retrieved instances, 4,367 real and 5,279 fake. Its Table 1 provenance is retained row by row below.

question_matrix.question: What operations, order and severity produce AncesTree?
question_matrix.finding: Each edge is a random crop→resize→lossy-compression pipeline. Crop probability is 50%, retaining 60–99.9% of image area, one dimension at a time; repeated edges can crop both dimensions. Resize probability is 60%, setting the shorter side in [256,2048] pixels, with Pillow/OpenCV and bilinear/bicubic/Lanczos interpolation chosen randomly. Compression probability is 95%, JPEG or WebP with format/QF distributions matched to the real-web collection; Figure 5 gives QF 50–100. JPEG encoders vary between Pillow and OpenCV. These are stochastic distributions, not five fixed scalar severity labels. Blur/noise/brightness/gamma in Figure 3 are illustrative IQA analyses, not additional stated AncesTree pipeline operations.
question_matrix.locator: Section 3 p.4; Figure 5 p.4; Figure 3 p.2 and Figure 4 p.3.

question_matrix.question: Is ancestry or an ordered version sequence explicitly represented?
question_matrix.finding: Yes for the in-lab construction: depth L=5, four first-level branches, then binary branching, yielding 4+8+16+32+64=124 descendants. The clean root is discarded from the reported dataset. Each branch/node has a known generated lineage and level in the construction; the L 1 oracle and level-conditioned detector plots use this structure. This does not establish that downloadable metadata includes a complete independently verified parent-edge annotation schema. ReWIND has source-group association but its actual web history/ancestors are explicitly unknown.
question_matrix.locator: Figure 5 p.4; Section 3 p.4; Figure 6 p.5; oracle protocol p.6/Table 2 p.7; ReWIND limitations p.8.

question_matrix.question: How are web repostings and near-duplicates collected?
question_matrix.finding: The authors repeat online searches for viral B-Free/FOSID seeds and add AMMeBa fact-checking images, RRDataset real news images and Google Fact Check Tools sources confirmed as AI-generated. Google Cloud Vision is used to find additional near-duplicates. They remove images whose shorter side is below 256 px and exact duplicates with equal MD 5, and retain source groups with at least 10 near-duplicates. Exact retrieval dates, query/result logs, completeness, human matching-error rates, per-file rights and exhaustive cross-source overlap controls are not specified in the manuscript.
question_matrix.locator: Section 3 pp.3–4; Table 1; footnotes 1–2 p.4; future retrieval-error analysis p.8.

question_matrix.question: How do real and simulated degradations differ?
question_matrix.finding: ReWIND consists of retrieved web files with unknown, potentially long and incomplete dissemination histories; earlier copies can disappear and timestamps can mislead. AncesTree is a simulated five-level process motivated by observed crop, format and JPEG-QF distributions. It allows controlled depth/oracle analyses, but cannot certify authentic upload order or reproduce every platform operation. The wild collection does not have known degradation-tree ground truth.

question_matrix.question: Are the resources substantively separate from QuAD training?
question_matrix.finding: The manuscript explicitly lists both resources as contributions and defines them in a separate data-construction section before the calibration method. It evaluates six public pretrained detectors, simple aggregation and quality/date/size selection as well as QuAD, so the resources can support analyses without training QuAD or accepting its Gaussian model. Around half of AncesTree is nevertheless used to fit QuAD calibration; the resource is not claimed to be wholly independent of the authors' experimental design. Scientific separability means reusable grouped data and controlled histories, not an external provenance or independent-team validation claim.
question_matrix.locator: Contribution list p.2; Section 3 pp.3–4; development fitting p.6; Sections 5/Tables 2–3 pp.6–8.

question_matrix.question: What are the split and leakage safeguards?
question_matrix.finding: Eight linear Gaussian calibration coefficients are maximum-likelihood fitted on around 50% of AncesTree, with remaining data for evaluation. The manuscript does not specify exact indices, random seed, source-group/semantic-family grouping, validation partition or whether near-duplicates of one source can cross development/test. It is unsafe to assume a leakage-free root-level split. On ReWIND, plain QuAD transfers AncesTree-fitted coefficients; QuAD* refits via leave-one-out on ReWIND. The leave-one-out unit and exact exclusion of related near-duplicates are not specified. MD 5 filtering is exact-file deduplication, not proof of cross-split content independence.
question_matrix.locator: Gaussian fitting p.6; Table 3 caption p.8; Section 3 deduplication p.4.

question_matrix.question: Is resource construction claimed as a substantive contribution?
question_matrix.finding: Yes. The p.2 contribution list separately identifies collection of the real-world ReWIND dataset and construction of the in-lab AncesTree dataset, alongside QuAD and detector evaluation. Section 3 provides quantitative curation/generation rules, source groups and known-versus-unknown histories. This is stronger R1 evidence than size or the abstract's public-availability assertion alone.
question_matrix.locator: Contribution list p.2; Section 3 pp.3–4; Table1/Figure5.

question_matrix.question: Can methods other than QuAD use the resources?
question_matrix.finding: Yes in the scientific design: six independent base detectors (DMID, CoDE, D 3, B-Free, DRCT, CO-SPY) are evaluated under random, naive aggregation, QF, size, IQA and, for the wild set, date selection. Figures 6/8 analyze version depth, quality ranking and missing instances. These are method-independent uses of grouped image data. No independently reproduced external research-team reuse was verified.

question_matrix.question: What release contents and licenses are independently established?
question_matrix.finding: The complete top README and successful API listings confirm public repository documentation and named CSV/code entries, not complete image or split contents. The README says calibration uses provided CSVs without dataset downloads. API lists AncesTree development/test/calibrated CSVs and source metadata, plus ReWIND score/calibration CSVs and AncesTree generation-script filenames. No CSV, image payload, script, NumPy array or archive body was downloaded. The two dataset README and full LICENSE.txt requests each timed out after 35 seconds with zero bytes and no retry. GitHub reports NOASSERTION, and the top README describes informational/nonprofit software use with all rights reserved. Full dataset/image rights, official split grouping, parent-edge schema and release completeness therefore remain unverified.
question_matrix.locator: Abstract p.1; root-owned top README and seven successful GitHub API/raw-text observations with preserved byte receipts; three failed text receipts in release_review.

question_matrix.question: Which experiments isolate degradation history or diversity benefits?
question_matrix.finding: Figure 6 stratifies detector distributions by known tree depth, showing increasing overlap. Figure 8 left compares QF/size/IQA ranking and number of selected instances; right varies available instance count, comparing all-logit mean, best 10 LoDa and QuAD. Tables 2–3 compare controlled versus genuinely retrieved web data and AncesTree-to-ReWIND calibration transfer versus ReWIND leave-one-out refitting. These show consequences of quality/history/availability, not a clean randomized dataset-diversity ablation or independent proof that extra sources alone cause the gains. Exact curve points beyond printed table/text values were not digitized.

question_matrix.question: What are baselines, metrics and quantitative findings?
question_matrix.finding: Metrics are balanced accuracy (percent) and negative log likelihood. All table cells are transcribed below. On AncesTree, mean naive aggregation is 73.2/0.75 versus QuAD 81.6/0.43 (+8.4 percentage points in bAcc). On ReWIND, naive is 63.0/1.27 versus transferred QuAD 70.3/0.63 (+7.3 points); earliest-date single selection 67.3/1.29 and QuAD*71.4/0.57 are distinct comparisons. Improvements are not universal: AncesTree B-Free QuAD 97.1 is below oracle 97.3 and LoDa 20 98.4; ReWIND CO-SPY QuAD 62.3/0.83 is worse than naive 65.7/0.81. QuAD* is not a held-out cross-dataset result.
question_matrix.locator: Tables2–3 pp.7–8; method configurations pp.6–7; Figure8 p.6.

question_matrix.question: What limitations constrain resource and release conclusions?
question_matrix.finding: AncesTree is simulated with only 100 real semantic roots and 1,000 generator counterparts; variants are correlated and not 136,400 independent scenes. ReWIND contains only 162 source groups, unknown generator/version histories and incomplete retrieval, fact-checking provenance dependencies, selection bias from the 10-copy/256 px filters and unknown rights/completeness. Gaussian conditional independence is an explicit approximation for correlated versions. Split grouping and ReWIND leave-one-out unit remain unverified. This is arXiv v1, not byte-verified CVPRW final; a scientific R1 contribution may be supported despite unverified public release and numerical reproduction.

current_canonical_bibliographic_record.abstract: The rapid advancement of text-to-image diffusion models has enabled the creation of highly photorealistic synthetic images that closely resemble real photographs, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic content from AI-generated fabrications. This poses challenges for cybersecurity, digital forensics, and disaster response, where fake imagery of floods, fires, or earthquakes can spread misinformation or disrupt emergency operations. To address this, we introduce Forged Calamity, a benchmark dataset for synthetic disaster detection containing 30,000 images, including 6,000 real and 24,000 synthetic samples generated by four diffusion models. Comprehensive experiments across fine-tuned and zero-shot settings reveal consistent weaknesses in current forensic approaches. Fine-tuned detectors perform well in-distribution but lose up to 50\% accuracy on unseen generators or disaster types, showing overfitting to model-specific artifacts. Zero-shot generalized detectors also struggle to maintain stable accuracy, with only limited resilience in a few representation-robust models. These findings highlight persistent generalization gaps and the urgent need for domain- and model-agnostic detection methods to ensure visual authenticity in the diffusion era.

question_matrix.question: Open-versus-closed generator evaluation

SD 1.5 fakes in the other categories are seen-generator/unseen-content tests; SD 2.0, SDXL and PixArt are generator-held-out relative to this narrow fine-tuning set. question_matrix.evidence_status_and_limit: Relative unseen-generator evaluation is supported; no source-attribution task change or universally clean open-world exposure claim is warranted.

curated:bb388762c1cb4bd3bf4a.title: Quality-Aware Calibration for AI-Generated Image Detection in the Wild
curated:bb388762c1cb4bd3bf4a.authors: Fabrizio Guillaro; Vincenzo De Rosa; Davide Cozzolino; Luisa Verdoliva
curated:bb388762c1cb4bd3bf4a.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition

curated:bb388762c1cb4bd3bf4a.abstract: Significant progress has been made in detecting synthetic images, however most existing approaches operate on a single image instance and overlook a key characteristic of real-world dissemination: as viral images circulate on the web, multiple near-duplicate versions appear and lose quality due to repeated operations like recompression, resizing and cropping. As a consequence, the same image may yield inconsistent forensic predictions based on which version has been analyzed. In this work, to address this issue we propose QuAD (Quality-Aware calibration with near-Duplicates) a novel framework that makes decisions based on all available near-duplicates of the same image. Given a query, we retrieve its online near-duplicates and feed them to a detector: the resulting scores are then aggregated based on the estimated quality of the corresponding instance. By doing so, we take advantage of all pieces of information while accounting for the reduced reliability of images impaired by multiple processing steps. To support large-scale evaluation, we introduce two datasets: AncesTree, an in-lab dataset of 136k images organized in stochastic degradation trees that simulate online reposting dynamics, and ReWIND, a real-world dataset of nearly 10k near-duplicate images collected from viral web content. Experiments on several state-of-the-art detectors show that our quality-aware fusion improves their performance consistently, with an average gain of around 8% in terms of balanced accuracy compared to plain average. Our results highlight the importance of jointly processing all the images available online to achieve reliable detection of AI-generated content in real-world applications. Code and data are publicly available at https://grip-unina.github.io/QuAD/

curated:5ad6cb3411820ff01a03.authors: Duc-Manh Phan; Quoc-Duy Tran; Duy-Khang Do; Anh-Tuan Vo; Hai-Dang Nguyen; Trong Le Do; Mai-Khiem Tran; Vinh-Tiep Nguyen; Tam V. Nguyen; Isao Echizen; Minh-Triet Tran; Trung-Nghia Le

curated:5ad6cb3411820ff01a03.abstract: The rapid advancement of text-to-image diffusion models has enabled the creation of highly photorealistic synthetic images that closely resemble real photographs, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic content from AI-generated fabrications. This poses challenges for cybersecurity, digital forensics, and disaster response, where fake imagery of floods, fires, or earthquakes can spread misinformation or disrupt emergency operations. To address this, we introduce Forged Calamity, a benchmark dataset for synthetic disaster detection containing 30,000 images, including 6,000 real and 24,000 synthetic samples generated by four diffusion models. Comprehensive experiments across fine-tuned and zero-shot settings reveal consistent weaknesses in current forensic approaches. Fine-tuned detectors perform well in-distribution but lose up to 50\% accuracy on unseen generators or disaster types, showing overfitting to model-specific artifacts. Zero-shot generalized detectors also struggle to maintain stable accuracy, with only limited resilience in a few representation-robust models. These findings highlight persistent generalization gaps and the urgent need for domain- and model-agnostic detection methods to ensure visual authenticity in the diffusion era.
